thesis: Spectacular prototypes can ratchet expectations while shifting verification costs.

ideas.statement: An expectations ratchet is a testable scenario, not a universal law.
Review bottlenecks and distribution of gains require measured deadlines and concrete acceptance criteria.

evidenceAndExamples.statement: In a fictional meeting, the manager sees a feature demonstrated in minutes and asks why delivery still requires two weeks. The team explains permissions, migration, tests, and compatibility. The explanations suddenly sound defensive. The prototype has created a new anchor: if it is visible, it is probably almost ready.

Sometimes the team really does overestimate the difficulty, and the new tool allows much faster delivery. At other times, the deadline is compressed on the strength of the most spectacular component, while less visible costs remain. We cannot decide from the demonstration’s appearance.

The 2024 Upwork survey included 2,500 respondents from the United States, United Kingdom, Australia, and Canada: business leaders, employees, and freelancers. Among employees using AI, 77% reported added work or reduced productivity in at least one way; 39% cited checking content, and 21% being asked to do more work. Meanwhile, 96% of executive-level leaders expected productivity gains. These are perceptions from a commercial survey, not causal measurements of time or proof that every firm shortened deadlines. [25]
Ranganathan and Ye also describe the intensification of assisted work. [26]

These signals justify investigating the difference between the tool’s promise and the worker’s experience. They do not justify a universal law that every automation makes life harder. Benefits can be distributed differently depending on organization and bargaining power.

Let us call the following scenario the “expectations ratchet”: an exceptional success is treated as the new standard, and the standard is extended to tasks where the advantage has not been demonstrated. When success repeats, the target rises. When it does not, the gap is attributed to the employee’s insufficient adaptation.

This is a possible mechanism, not a causal conclusion established for every company. It should be sought in the data: how are estimates changed, what tasks are compared, how are exceptions treated, and who bears the planning errors?

The ratchet can also be personal. A founder sees that they can build a demonstration in an evening and adds two more initiatives. No superior imposes the deadline. Yet the tool’s new power becomes a new obligation to oneself. Instead of “I can do more,” there appears “I should do more, otherwise I am wasting an opportunity.”

An observational analysis by Xu and colleagues of open-source projects reports that the benefits of assisted contributions can coexist with additional maintenance and review tasks for core developers. The paper is a preprint, and causal interpretation requires caution. The organizationally relevant idea is that producing a contribution and absorbing it into a project do not necessarily benefit the same person. [29]

Imagine a team where ten people each submit twice as many changes, but only two can perform security reviews. More material does not automatically mean more safe deliveries. It may mean a longer queue, rushed evaluation, or pressure to lower the standard.

In a simplified numerical example, if agents produce twenty proposals per hour and the team can rigorously check five, the difference accumulates if every proposal enters the workflow. This is not a lack of enthusiasm. It is a mismatch in capacity.

There are several legitimate answers. The customer can receive a better product. The firm can reduce costs. The worker can have more time. The team can invest in testing or new projects. Technology does not choose the distribution on its own.

That is why the promise “AI will free you” is incomplete without a sentence about the right to keep part of the gain. If every saving immediately becomes an additional requirement, a person can become more efficient and more exhausted at the same time.

A reasonable organizational practice would be to recalibrate deadlines after measurements across task classes, not after the best demonstration. The estimate must include verification and uncertainty. An ambitious deadline is not inherently abusive; it becomes unhealthy when it is immune to data and every hidden cost is attributed to the person who makes it visible.

This sentence will become more important in a world that quickly generates the appearance of completion. It must not be a refuge for unlimited perfectionism. It must be tied to concrete criteria: what property is missing, what risk remains, and what evidence will close the task?

A mature team rewards more than the person who produces the first version. It also rewards the person who can demonstrate why that version deserves acceptance. Otherwise, society will produce more and more things that look finished and less and less time to find out whether they are.

objectionsAndQualifications.statement: Commercial survey perceptions and observational preprint do not prove universal causality.

audit.notes: Complete chapter read; preserve proposed concepts, empirical limits and non-diagnostic distinctions.
